body:
The Importance of Ceramics

Pottery was one of the most widespread Harappan crafts. People required vessels for preparing food, storing grain, carrying water and performing other household activities.

Harappan craftspeople produced vessels in a wide range of shapes and sizes. Their products included plain everyday pottery, painted vessels, large storage jars, bowls, dishes and smaller containers.

Ceramics are objects made from clay or other suitable mineral materials that become hard through heating. Pottery is a major category of ceramics.

Manufacture of Harappan Pottery

Harappan pottery was commonly produced using a potter's wheel, although hand-made vessels and vessels completed through a combination of techniques also existed.

Clay was shaped into the desired vessel, sometimes with the aid of a rotating wheel. The vessel was then dried and fired so that it became hard and durable.

Large vessels could require techniques different from those used for smaller pots. A vessel might be partly formed by hand and then finished on a wheel.

Plain Pottery

Plain pottery was more common than elaborately painted pottery. Much of it was made from reddish clay, sometimes with a surface coating called a slip.

A slip is a thin preparation of fine clay and water applied to a vessel's surface before firing. It can produce a smoother finish and help create a more uniform surface colour.

Black-Painted Red Ware

One of the best-known Harappan pottery traditions is red pottery decorated with black designs.

The vessel was generally given a reddish surface coating, and designs were painted in black before firing. Common decorative elements included geometric patterns, intersecting circles, plant forms and animal motifs.

The presence of similar pottery styles across many settlements indicates shared craft traditions and recognisable forms of production.

Other Pottery Types

Harappan ceramic production also included vessels with incised decoration, perforated vessels and occasional multicoloured designs.

Incised decoration consists of lines or patterns cut into a surface. Polychrome pottery uses several colours, but such pottery was comparatively uncommon.

Perforated Pottery

Some Harappan vessels had numerous holes in their walls and sometimes a larger opening at the bottom. These are known as perforated vessels.

Such vessels may have been used to strain liquids or separate substances. Their exact functions are not completely established, so they should not be assigned one exclusive use in every context.

Terracotta Objects

Terracotta means fired clay. Harappan craftspeople used this material to produce objects beyond ordinary cooking and storage pottery.

Terracotta objects included figurines of people and animals, toy carts, wheels, rattles, whistles, bangles and other small items.

These objects demonstrate the versatility of clay as a material. It could be shaped into containers, models, ornaments and objects used in daily life.

Terracotta models are also historically useful because some represent objects made from less durable materials. For example, a terracotta plough model helps establish that the agricultural implement was known even though the original wooden equipment has not survived.

Faience: An Artificially Produced Material

Faience was another important Harappan craft material. Unlike ordinary stone or shell, it was produced through a specialised process using finely powdered mineral ingredients.

Harappan faience was commonly prepared from powdered quartz or other silica-rich material mixed with suitable substances that enabled shaping and glazing during firing.

The finished objects often had a shiny surface, commonly blue or blue-green in colour.

Uses of Faience

Faience was used to make:

  • Beads and small ornaments.
  • Bangles and earrings.
  • Miniature vessels.
  • Other decorative and specialised objects.

Manufacturing faience required specialised knowledge of mineral ingredients, shaping and heating. The finished material could imitate the appearance of attractive stones while being manufactured from prepared ingredients.

Distinguish the materials

Terracotta is fired clay. Faience is an artificially prepared, silica-rich material that develops a glazed surface. Both involve heating, but they are not the same material.

Firing and Specialised Production

Harappan craftspeople used controlled heating for ceramic production. The temperature and firing conditions affected the hardness, colour and finish of the final objects.

Pottery production required skills in selecting suitable clay, shaping vessels, preparing surfaces and firing them. Faience manufacture required additional control over mineral ingredients and surface glazing.

These crafts illustrate an important feature of Harappan technology: craftspeople could transform inexpensive or locally available raw materials into durable products requiring considerable technical skill.

Prelims focus

  • Harappan pottery was predominantly wheel-made, although hand-made pottery also existed.
  • Plain pottery was more common than painted pottery.
  • Red pottery with black painted designs was a characteristic Harappan ceramic tradition.
  • Perforated vessels may have served as strainers.
  • Terracotta means fired clay.
  • Trap: Faience is an artificially manufactured glazed material, not a naturally occurring semiprecious stone.

[NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 2, Arts of the Indus Valley, pp. 11–15, sections Terracotta and Pottery; NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, Chapter 4, pp. 36–37, section Faience; V. N. Prabhakar, Protohistory of India and Pakistan III: Indus Crafts and Arts, INFLIBNET, sections 2.1, Ceramics, and 2.8, Faience Objects, accessed 17 November 2026.]

body:
Craft Specialisation in Harappan Society

The Harappans produced ornaments and other objects from a remarkable variety of materials. Some crafts required particular tools, extensive experience and carefully controlled processes.

Craft specialisation means that certain people developed expertise in making particular kinds of objects. Specialisation could occur in households, workshops or settlements strongly associated with particular industries.

Bead-making and shell working provide important examples of this development.

Materials Used for Beads

Harappan craftspeople made beads from stones, metals and other materials.

Material groupExamplesUse
Semiprecious stonesCarnelian, jasper, agate and lapis lazuliDecorative and specialised beads
Other stonesCrystal, quartz and steatiteBeads of different sizes and shapes
MetalsCopper, bronze and goldBeads and ornament components
Other materialsShell, faience and terracottaBangles, beads and additional ornaments

Beads could be spherical, cylindrical, disc-shaped, barrel-shaped or segmented. Some were made by joining different materials. Others were decorated by painting, incising or etching.

Carnelian Bead-Making

Carnelian is a reddish variety of chalcedony, a mineral related to quartz. It was an important material for Harappan bead production.

Carnelian beads are particularly significant for Gujarat because sources of carnelian and related stones were available in the region around present-day Bharuch and the surrounding areas.

Production Process

Making a finished carnelian bead involved several stages:

  1. Obtain raw stone: Select suitable nodules or pieces of agate or carnelian.
  2. Apply heat when required: Heating could transform the appearance of yellowish raw material and enhance the characteristic reddish colour.
  3. Roughly shape the material: Chip away unwanted portions of stone.
  4. Refine the shape: Use controlled flaking, grinding and polishing to produce the desired form.
  5. Drill a hole: Perforate the bead so that a thread or cord can pass through it.
  6. Finish and decorate: Complete polishing and, where required, add etched or other decorative designs.

Heating was particularly important for producing the desired colour in some carnelian materials. Drilling hard stone required specialised implements and technical skill.

Specialised Drills

Evidence of specialised drilling equipment has been recovered from Chanhudaro, Lothal and Dholavira.

Such implements indicate that making fine stone beads was more complicated than simply collecting and polishing naturally attractive stones.

Steatite Beads

Steatite, commonly called soapstone, is relatively soft and can be worked more easily than many hard stones.

Harappan craftspeople also prepared some beads from a paste made with powdered steatite. This enabled the production of small and varied shapes.

Very small steatite beads demonstrate considerable manufacturing skill. Their production should not be confused with the process used to shape harder carnelian beads.

Major Bead-Making Centres

Chanhudaro

Chanhudaro, in present-day Pakistan, was a notable specialised craft settlement. It covered less than 7 hectares, compared with approximately 125 hectares at Mohenjodaro.

Activities associated with Chanhudaro included bead-making, shell cutting, metalworking, seal-making and weight-making.

The settlement is especially significant because craft production occupied a prominent place in its economy.

Lothal

Lothal in Gujarat was another important centre of bead production.

Excavations revealed a building interpreted as a bead-making workshop. Finds included stone pieces, beads at different stages of manufacture, finished beads, production waste, tools and associated heating facilities.

The original excavation report describes a jar containing approximately 600 finished carnelian beads in the workshop area, together with other material associated with bead production.

These discoveries establish a clear connection between Lothal and specialised manufacturing.

Dholavira

Dholavira in Kachchh also yielded evidence of bead processing and other specialised crafts. Tools, workshop areas and finished objects demonstrate that sophisticated production was carried out at this Gujarat settlement.

Shell Craft

Shells obtained from coastal areas were worked into ornaments and useful objects. Shell working required knowledge of cutting, grinding and polishing because some marine shells are hard and difficult to shape.

Important shell products included:

  • Bangles and other ornaments.
  • Beads and decorative pieces.
  • Ladles.
  • Inlay pieces used to decorate other objects.

Nageshwar and Balakot

Nageshwar in Gujarat and Balakot in present-day Pakistan were coastal settlements associated with specialised shell production.

Their location near marine resources made shell procurement easier. Finished shell objects could then be supplied to settlements farther inland.

How Specialists Obtained Raw Materials

Not all craft materials were available near the settlements where finished goods were produced.

Lothal was situated near sources of carnelian, steatite and other materials in Gujarat and neighbouring regions. Other valuable stones, including lapis lazuli, could come from much farther away.

Harappan settlements and contacts connected regions possessing raw materials with settlements possessing specialised production skills.

Why Some Settlements Were Craft Centres

A specialised centre could develop where raw materials were accessible, skilled workers were available, or finished goods could be supplied to larger markets.

However, craft production was not confined to a few small centres. Large cities such as Harappa and Mohenjodaro also contained evidence of manufacturing.

Prelims focus

  • Chanhudaro: specialised settlement associated with bead-making and several other crafts.
  • Lothal: bead-making workshop and associated tools and materials.
  • Dholavira: bead processing and other specialist crafts.
  • Nageshwar and Balakot: important shell-working centres.
  • Carnelian could acquire its characteristic reddish colour through controlled heating.
  • Trap: Bead-making was not limited to carnelian; Harappan beads were produced from many stones, metals, shell, terracotta and faience.

[NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, pp. 10–12, sections 5 and 6.1; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 2, Arts of the Indus Valley, pp. 13–15, section Beads and Ornaments; Archaeological Survey of India, S. R. Rao, Lothal: A Harappan Port Town (1955–62), Volume I, 1979, Chapter VII, pp. 118–119, section Bead Factory; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Dholavira: a Harappan City, Brief Synthesis and Authenticity, accessed 17 November 2026.]
